newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen leader orders halt to Russian talks.
newsitem.headline: Chechen leader orders halt to Russian talks.

text.p: The president of Russia's separatist region of Chechnya on Tuesday ordered a halt to all talks with Moscow until Russia approved a plan to revitalise Chechnya's economy, which was devastated by 20 months of war.

"President Aslan Maskhadov has banned all ministers' trips to Moscow and all talks with Russian officials until a plan to rebuild Chechnya is signed," Maskhadov's spokesman Kazbek Khadzhiyev told Reuters in the Chechen capital, Grozny.

The halt could jeopardise talks on renovating a pipeline through which early oil from Azerbaijan's new offshore deposits is expected to run to world markets through Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiisk this autumn.

In a sign of improving relations, Russian and Chechen officials signed a deal earlier this month detailing how they would repair the war-damaged pipeline that runs across Chechnya. But many aspects of the accord remain unsettled.

The issue is crucial for the two sides and they are interested in solving the problem as soon as possible, as the oil is expected to provide both Russia and Chechnya with generous revenues in transport fees.

Interfax news agency said Maskhadov on Monday met the Grozny representative of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and complained Moscow was not fulfilling treaties signed earlier.
He also asked the OSCE for broader aid to Chechnya.

Interfax quoted Ivan Rybkin, Secretary of Russian President Boris Yeltsin's Security Council, as saying the Moscow government and Chechen authorities had never stopped working on rebuilding Chechnya's economy "and never would stop, not even for a minute".
He did not say, however, when he expected the concrete reconstruction plan to be approved and the work to start.

Chechen leaders, who signed a ceasefire with Moscow last August after ousting Russian troops from Grozny, insist that their Moslem southern region is independent from Russia. Under a peace pact, the question of formal sovereignty was set aside.
The Kremlin views Chechnya as an integral part of the Russian Federation and has pledged to plough in funds to rebuild its economy and infrastructure.

Although never spelled out, many analysts see the promise of funds as a quid pro quo for the Chechens dropping demands for recognition of their sovereignty. Maskhadov, seen as a moderate in Moscow, won a presidential election in January.
